chapter: Postwar years, accident and lean times
title: Gigging around New York; Red Richards takes him to Europe in 1968
summary: After Philadelphia he did club dates at places like Eddie Condon's and Jimmy Ryan's; in 1968 Red Richards's Saints and Sinners took him to Europe for the first time, where people knew him from Fats.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Well, okay, so your Philadelphia job is going because they tore down the building. What did you do next?
Well, from there, let me see. What did I do?
Gigged a bit, I guess.
Gigged a bit, yeah, with this group, that group. Working down Eddie Condon's, here and there, and with different groups.
Jimmy Ryan?
Jimmy Ryan's, aw, and then one night -- I mean what you call them, club dates here and there. Oh, with Red Richards. Oh!
Is this where you met Red?
Oh, oh, oh. About to forget, the very important --
Okay.
That's very important, Red, because with all the big bands I had been with, none of them were able
to take me to Europe. But Red did. He promised me, and asked me if I wanted to go. And in fact, this was after I had had pneumonia.
When --

I'm trying to think now when the hell was that, because he called me and asked me to go, and I said I'm sorry, I can't. I just got out of bed with pneumonia, but I would love to, and so forth. And I said but hope it happens the next time, so another time when he called me, I was ready. I told him I would try it.

And I got myself together. We went -- went to Europe, and I started thinking about Fats, Claude Hopkins, Stuff Smith, all of them, I mean people with bigger than big names and Red Richards right riches, and as far as name, I mean, he -- you know, Saints and Sinners.
But this was much later, wasn't it?
Oh, much later. I mean nothing, that's what I'm saying. You know. In a way he was nobody. I mean compared with the other big guys, you know? He took me to Europe, and was a very, very nice tour.
This was the first time you'd been to Europe?
The first time. You know?
This was when? In the sixties?
Uh, no. I don't know -- yeah.
: In the 1960's.

'68. '68. Yeah, uh-huh. And I mean things began to happen, and a lot of people, they had heard of me with Pats. They were waiting, you know, want to see what I looked like, and Mr. Autrey, I've been hearing you, so forth and so on, and now it's a pleasure to see you in person. When they heard -- a lot of them heard about me writing the book, my book, which should be -- would be on the way. They got more excited.
(Laughter.)

I got excited, and another thing, sickness, another thing set in, and it hampered my ideas and my writing, and whatnot, so I had to slow down and wait and wait and wait and wait, one of those things. You know?
